items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I loved him, he was a good friend of mine.

ctx.x: And it’s like a vocabulary lesson in what was happening at the time. I mean what do they call this, this kind of language? Or maybe it didn’t have a name? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

Then it didn’t have a name. Leonard Feather gave it the name “vocalese.” And that stuck. But Ralph Gleason, when he was writing for the San Francisco Chronicle, wrote a wonderful column on what you just remarked on. He said some day in the future, sociologists will refer to Jon Hendricks’ lyrics to see how people spoke in the 50s and 60s. And I thought — I was very flattered by that. It was very flattering. But I think it’s true. Because the lyrics are full of vulgate expressions that were very much in use at one…
And you had quite a wonderful association with Count Basie.

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: which is what Leonard Feather dubbed “vocalese”

ctx.x: Yeah, that’s a phenomenon I’m very happy I lived to see because being in show business, since seven, there are things that you see that you expect to see. You expect it if you do well in your act, people will give you applause and they’ll love you and they’ll want you to come back. This you expect. But I never saw what happened when Annie Ross and I got back together. And that is, the minute we were introduced and walked on stage, the whole house stood up and applauded for 12-15 minutes. And I never saw this in…

It sure did, and it lasted. I mean that music has been out there for some 40 years now, and hit on different generations, and I think people responded to the quality and the longevity of it, and thus that kind of ovation.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Leonard Feather went with him. Leonard Feather told me, when they got off the plane, the first thing the Russian journalists said was, “Why didn’t you send Duke Ellington?”

ctx.x: So during the – the ’60s was a very fertile period.

Yeah, it was. It was – well, that hasn’t been reported yet. I told you that I studied law and my major was English and my minor was history. As a person interested in history, I’m amazed how that whole phenomena has not been covered by historians. It brings up again the true sickness that this country suffers from its racism. It prevents it from looking at life and seeing things as it truly is, because that whole rock movement, that whole exodus of masses of white children from their homes to receptive cities…
